one_liner: Tiny embeddable class-based scripting VM in C; fastest on method-dispatch benchmarks, slower than Lua 5.4 elsewhere.
what_it_does: Wren is a dynamically typed, class-based scripting language with fibers, implemented as a small VM in C (README: under 4,000 semicolons) meant for embedding in applications. The host creates a VM with wrenNewVM(&config), runs source with wrenInterpret(vm, module, source), calls Wren methods through handles (wrenMakeCallHandle/wrenCall) and exchanges values through a slot API; host functionality is exposed as foreign methods and classes. It is a different language and C API from Lua or Python, not a drop-in replacement.
how_it_is_fast: Values are NaN-tagged 8-byte doubles, so numbers, bools and null are unboxed. Classes are declared statically with private fields, so field access is a fixed slot offset known at compile time, and copy-down inheritance plus arity-overloaded signatures make a method call a single lookup in the receiver class's method table with no argument-count check. The interpreter loop uses computed-goto dispatch on GCC/Clang (author: 5-10% gain; switch fallback on MSVC), and a Lua-style single-pass compiler emits bytecode while parsing.
when_to_use: Embedded scripting dominated by object method calls and dynamic dispatch: on an independent 2023 re-run (Ryzen 9 5950X) method_call took 0.079 s vs Lua 5.4.4 0.121 s, Ruby 3.0.5 0.104 s, Python 3.11.3 0.171 s.
Games or apps that want a class-based language with fibers in a VM small enough to read and patch, on platforms where JIT compilation is not allowed.
Hosts that run several isolated interpreters at once: the C implementation has no global state, so separate VMs can run concurrently on different threads.
Projects that need to compile the interpreter as C99 or C++98 with no dependencies beyond the C standard library (and libm).
when_not_to_use: Recursion- or arithmetic-heavy scripts: in the same 2023 re-run Lua 5.4.4 ran recursive Fibonacci in 0.087 s vs Wren 0.148 s, and an i7-12700H run (discussion #1183) had Lua 5.4.6 at 0.085 s vs Wren 0.131 s and 0.33 s vs 0.56 s on the for-loop benchmark.
Allocation-heavy code: on binary trees Wren 0.4 (0.141 s) was slower than Lua 5.4 (0.139 s), Python 3.11 (0.137 s), Ruby 3.0 (0.116 s) and LuaJIT -joff (0.074 s) in the 2023 re-run.
Hash maps with numeric keys: discussion #1183 measured map_numeric at 0.728 s for Wren vs 0.431 s for CPython 3.9.18.

Running untrusted script source: five fuzzer-reported memory-safety bugs in the compiler (heap/stack/global buffer overflows, NULL dereference; issues #1217-#1221, January 2026) are open, and deep recursion is not checked (issue #939: memory grows until the OOM killer sends SIGKILL).

When you need a large ecosystem or standard library, or a JIT: Wren has a small standard library (README), and LuaJIT even in -joff mode beat it on binary trees and Fibonacci in both the original and the 2023 runs.

integration.dependencies: none beyond the C standard library; libm must be linked explicitly on Linux and BSD
integration.min_toolchain: C99 or C++98; computed-goto dispatch needs GCC or Clang (disabled for MSVC without clang)
integration.platforms: any platform with IEEE-754 doubles (NaN tagging; WREN_NAN_TAGGING=0 switches to a larger struct representation)
integration.thread_safety: No global state; multiple VMs can run concurrently on different threads. Sharing one VM across threads is not documented as safe.

gotchas: Harness flaws behind the published numbers: the page (doc/site/performance.markdown) uses about-2014 baselines (Lua 5.2.3, Python 2.7.5/3.3.4, Ruby 2.0.0) and best-of-10 times; each script times itself with a different clock (Wren clock()/CLOCKS_PER_SEC, Lua os.clock and Python time.process_time are CPU time, Ruby Time.now is wall time); the current .py scripts call time.process_time (changed by PR #844 in 2021), which Python 2.7 does not have, so the page's Python 2.7.5 rows cannot be reproduced with today's scripts; DeltaBlue exists only for Wren, Python and Dart (delta_blue.lua.inprogress), so its win is over Python only.
The map_numeric benchmark is not like-for-like against Lua: the Lua script fills keys 1..2,000,000 in order, which Lua stores in a table's array part, while Wren uses its hash Map.

A refreshed performance page with modern baselines (PR #1164 by asb, Ryzen 9 5950X, median of 10, Lua 5.4.4, LuaJIT 2.1.0-beta3, Python 3.11.3, Ruby 3.0.5) has been open and unreviewed since 2023-04-10; it keeps Wren's method-call and DeltaBlue wins but shows Wren slowest on binary trees and behind Lua 5.4 and Ruby 3.0 on Fibonacci.

The embedding API is unchecked in release builds (wrong slot or argument counts are undefined behaviour), calling a Wren method handle from inside a foreign method is an open issue (#1169), and hard limits apply: 16 parameters per method, 255 fields per class, 65,536 module variables (wren_common.h).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Wren over LuaJIT or pocketpy when you want a class-based language with fibers in a tiny VM and your scripts are dominated by method calls, where it beat LuaJIT -joff, Lua 5.4 and CPython 3.11; for numeric, recursive or allocation-heavy scripts LuaJIT (even with the JIT off) or plain Lua 5.4 is faster.
verified_claims_summary: On the author's 2.3 GHz Core i7 MacBook Pro (no compiler or flags stated, best of 10, startup excluded) Wren beat Lua 5.2.3, Python 2.7.5/3.3.4 and Ruby 2.0.0 on method call (0.12 s vs Lua 0.35 s), DeltaBlue (Python only), binary trees and Fibonacci, while LuaJIT 2.0.2 -joff won binary trees and Fibonacci. An independent 2023 re-run on a Ryzen 9 5950X against Lua 5.4.4, Python 3.11.3 and Ruby 3.0.5 keeps only the method-call (0.079 s vs Lua 0.121 s) and DeltaBlue (0.086 s vs Python 0.107 s) wins.
status_note: Slow-moving but not abandoned: latest release still 0.4.0, commits only in February-March 2025 and November 2025 after a gap since September 2022, MIT and easy to vendor; the headline speed claim holds only against the old baselines and should be narrowed to method dispatch against current Lua, Python and Ruby.
